claim: Oscillatory brain activity reflects different internal brain states including neurons' excitatory state and synchrony among neurons.
source: Oscillatory brain activity reflects different internal brain states including neurons' excitatory state and synchrony among neurons.
evidence: This is a general statement about oscillatory brain activity presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study, but draws on established scientific understanding.

claim: Different oscillations are often coupled, such as gamma oscillations nested in theta in the hippocampus.
source: However, characterizing these states is complicated by the fact that different oscillations are often coupled, such as gamma oscillations nested in theta in the hippocampus, and changes in coupling are thought to reflect distinct states.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about theta-gamma coupling in the hippocampus.

claim: Four theta-gamma coupling states were identified in rat hippocampal CA1.
source: Using this method, we identified four theta-gamma coupling states in rat hippocampal CA1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the clustering analysis performed on experimental data.

claim: The four theta-gamma coupling states differed in abundance across behaviors.
source: These states differed in abundance across behaviors, phase synchrony with other hippocampal subregions, and neural coding properties suggesting that these states are functionally distinct.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing state occurrences across different behavioral conditions.

claim: The four theta-gamma coupling states differed in phase synchrony with other hippocampal subregions.
source: These states differed in abundance across behaviors, phase synchrony with other hippocampal subregions, and neural coding properties suggesting that these states are functionally distinct.
evidence: This claim is supported by pairwise phase consistency (PPC) analysis between CA1 and CA3/EC shown in the results.

claim: The four theta-gamma coupling states differed in neural coding properties.
source: These states differed in abundance across behaviors, phase synchrony with other hippocampal subregions, and neural coding properties suggesting that these states are functionally distinct.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of spatial information and phase precession across different TG states.

claim: Frequent switching between theta-gamma states occurs from one theta cycle to the next.
source: We captured cycle-to-cycle changes in oscillatory coupling states and found frequent switching between theta-gamma states showing that the hippocampus rapidly shifts between different functional states.
evidence: This is supported by the Markov chain analysis of state transitions showing transition probabilities ranging from 0.15 to 0.36.

claim: Oscillations reflect rhythmic fluctuations in excitability.
source: Furthermore, oscillatory activity serves as a read-out of internal network states: oscillations (typically recorded extracellularly) reflect rhythmic fluctuations in excitability, and therefore periods during which neurons are more or less likely to respond to excitatory inputs by generating action potentials (Cardin, 2016; Fries, 2015; Roberts et al., 2013; Rohenkohl et al., 2018; Sohal, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Different frequencies of oscillations have been proposed to route communication between different subregions of the hippocampus.
source: In fact, different frequencies of oscillations have been proposed to route communication between different subregions of the hippocampus (Colgin, 2011; Colgin et al., 2009; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2016; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Current methods to assess oscillatory activity average neural signals over long consecutive time periods, obscuring moment-to-moment changes.
source: However, current methods to assess oscillatory activity average neural signals over long consecutive time periods (Canolty et al., 2006; Le Van Quyen and Bragin, 2007), obscuring moment-to-moment changes in these signals that may indicate rapid changes in communication between brain regions (Huys et al., 2014; Tognoli and Kelso, 2009).
evidence: This is a critique of existing methods supported by citations.

claim: Faster oscillations are often nested in slower oscillations with the faster oscillations appearing at a particular phase of the slower oscillation.
source: Faster oscillations are often nested in slower oscillations with the faster oscillations appearing at a particular phase of the slower oscillation (Canolty and Knight, 2010; Jirsa and Müller, 2013), such as gamma (30–150 Hz) nested in theta (6–12 Hz) in the hippocampus (HPC), parietal cortex and prefrontal cortex (PFC), as well as delta (4 Hz)-gamma (30–100 Hz) coupling in PFC and ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Buzsáki et al., 2003; Fujisawa and Buzsaki, 2011; Scheffzük et al., 2011; Sirota et al., 2008; Tamura et al., 2017; Tort et al., 2013; Tort et al., 2009; Tort et al., 2008; Trimper et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Three subtypes of gamma oscillations (30–150 Hz), characterized by different frequency content, nest in different phases of theta oscillations (6–12 Hz) in hippocampal CA1.
source: Three subtypes of gamma oscillations (30–150 Hz), characterized by different frequency content, nest in different phases of theta oscillations (6–12 Hz) in hippocampal CA1 (Amemiya and Redish, 2018; Andersen et al., 2006; Buzsáki, 2006; Colgin et al. (2009); Klausberger and Somogyi (2008); Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2016; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Slow gamma (30–50 Hz) is dominant in stratum radiatum.
source: Slow gamma (30–50 Hz), which is dominant in stratum (str.) radiatum (rad), is associated with input from the CA3 subregion of HPC and is thought to play a role in memory retrieval (Bieri et al., 2014; Colgin, 2015a; Igarashi et al., 2014; Tort et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Slow gamma is associated with input from the CA3 subregion of HPC.
source: Slow gamma (30–50 Hz), which is dominant in stratum (str.) radiatum (rad), is associated with input from the CA3 subregion of HPC and is thought to play a role in memory retrieval (Bieri et al., 2014; Colgin, 2015a; Igarashi et al., 2014; Tort et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Slow gamma is thought to play a role in memory retrieval.
source: Slow gamma (30–50 Hz), which is dominant in stratum (str.) radiatum (rad), is associated with input from the CA3 subregion of HPC and is thought to play a role in memory retrieval (Bieri et al., 2014; Colgin, 2015a; Igarashi et al., 2014; Tort et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Medium gamma (60–120 Hz) is most active in stratum lacunosum-moleculare.
source: Medium gamma (60–120 Hz), which is most active in str. lacunosum-moleculare (lm), is associated with input from layer III of the entorhinal cortex (EC3) and is thought to encode ongoing sensory information (Bieri et al., 2014; Cabral et al., 2014; Newman et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Medium gamma is associated with input from layer III of the entorhinal cortex (EC3).
source: Medium gamma (60–120 Hz), which is most active in str. lacunosum-moleculare (lm), is associated with input from layer III of the entorhinal cortex (EC3) and is thought to encode ongoing sensory information (Bieri et al., 2014; Cabral et al., 2014; Newman et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Medium gamma is thought to encode ongoing sensory information.
source: Medium gamma (60–120 Hz), which is most active in str. lacunosum-moleculare (lm), is associated with input from layer III of the entorhinal cortex (EC3) and is thought to encode ongoing sensory information (Bieri et al., 2014; Cabral et al., 2014; Newman et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Fast gamma (>120 Hz) is thought to represent local neural activity in stratum pyramidal of CA1.
source: Fast gamma (>120 Hz), is thought to represent local neural activity in str. pyramidal (pyr) of CA1 (Schomburg et al., 2014; Sullivan et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Prior work has hypothesized that CA1 rapidly shifts between inputs from CA3 and inputs from EC.
source: Indeed, prior work has hypothesized that CA1 rapidly shifts between inputs from CA3, which are thought important for memory retrieval, and inputs from EC, which are thought to process ongoing sensory experiences.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work that is being tested in this study.

claim: If rapid shifts between CA3 and EC inputs occur, they would be reflected by rapid shifts between different types of gamma from one theta cycle to the next.
source: If such rapid shifts occur, they would be reflected by rapid shifts between different types of gamma from one theta cycle to the next (Gupta et al., 2012; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Hasselmo and Stern, 2014; Mizuseki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on prior hypotheses, supported by citations.

claim: The study used a two-step analysis method to track individual theta cycles based on gamma frequency content and gamma's preferred phase of theta.
source: In this paper, we describe a novel two-step analysis method to track individual theta cycles based on gamma frequency content and gamma's preferred phase of theta.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The clustering phase used signal processing and machine learning methods.
source: First, we cluster theta-gamma coupling into different states using signal processing and machine learning methods.
evidence: This describes the methods used in the first phase of analysis.

claim: The second phase tracked moment-to-moment changes in theta-gamma coupling following Markov processes using random process theory.
source: Second, we track moment-to-moment changes in theta-gamma coupling following Markov processes using random process theory.
evidence: This describes the methods used in the second phase of analysis.

claim: Four theta-gamma coupling states were found without assuming the number of states that exist.
source: In the clustering phase, we found four theta-gamma coupling states without assuming the number of states that exist.
evidence: This describes a key finding and methodological feature of the clustering approach.

claim: The four states correspond to both previously reported theta-gamma coupling (slow, medium, and fast gamma) and new states (two distinct fast gammas).
source: These four states correspond to both previously reported theta-gamma coupling, namely slow, medium, and fast gamma (Colgin et al., 2009; Schomburg et al., 2014), and new states, namely two distinct fast gammas.
evidence: This claim compares the findings to prior research and identifies novel findings.

claim: Rapid changes in theta-gamma coupling states occur from one theta cycle to the next.
source: We found rapid changes in theta-gamma coupling states from one theta cycle to the next.
evidence: This is a key finding from the Markov chain analysis.

claim: Neural codes, specifically spatial information and phase precession, differed across the identified theta-gamma states.
source: Finally, we found neural codes, specifically spatial information and phase precession differed across the identified theta-gamma states (TG states), supporting that these states have distinct functional roles.
evidence: This is a finding from the neural coding analysis.

claim: The theta-gamma coupling states in CA1 have distinct pairwise phase consistency (PPC) with other hippocampal subregions.
source: Indeed, these theta-gamma coupling states in CA1 have distinct pairwise phase consistency (PPC) with other hippocampal subregions and abundance during different behaviors and REM sleep.
evidence: This is a finding from the PPC analysis.

claim: The theta-gamma coupling states have distinct abundance during different behaviors and REM sleep.
source: Indeed, these theta-gamma coupling states in CA1 have distinct pairwise phase consistency (PPC) with other hippocampal subregions and abundance during different behaviors and REM sleep.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral state analysis.

claim: CA1 rapidly shifts between four theta-gamma coupling states that likely reflect distinct computational processes in the hippocampus.
source: Together these results reveal that CA1 rapidly shifts between four theta-gamma coupling states that likely reflect distinct computational processes in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the combined findings of the study.

claim: K-means clustering with k determined by community clustering was used to categorize FPPs into 4 TG coupling states.
source: We applied k-means clustering with k determined by community clustering to categorize FPPs into 4 TG coupling states (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the specific clustering method used.

claim: All clusters of FPP detected across recording sites had high within-group correlations over time.
source: All clusters of FPP detected across recording sites had high within-group correlations over time showing that TG state categorization was similar across channels over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B right panel).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The results generated by the k-means method with four clusters were highly robust across all recording sites within the pyramidal layer.
source: The results generated by the k-means method with four clusters, were highly robust across all recording sites within the pyramidal layer.
evidence: This describes the robustness of the clustering method.

claim: The peak frequency of the 'medium' gamma band became higher on recording sites toward the stratum oriens side of the pyramidal layer.
source: Based on our observation, however, the peak frequency of the 'medium' gamma band (second column in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, right panel) became higher (as high as high gamma) on recording sites toward the stratum oriens side of the pyramidal layer.
evidence: This observation is based on data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Data recorded near the pyramidal layer center or below (toward stratum radiatum side) should be used for this analysis method to preserve the frequency characteristics of 'medium gamma'.
source: Thus, we suggest using data recorded near the pyramidal layer center or below (toward stratum radiatum side) for this analysis method to preserve the frequency characteristics of 'medium gamma'.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the observations.

claim: Four clusters were found in all rats during awake periods.
source: In all rats during awake periods, we found four clusters (Figure 1F) that differed significantly from the other clusters in terms of preferred frequency (p < 0.001, F3, 210 (gamma states)=1160.02, one-way ANOVA repeated Measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for six comparisons) and/or theta phase (Parametric Watson-Williams multi-sample test (Berens, 2009); q < 0.05, FDR correction for six comparisons)
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The four clusters differed significantly from each other in terms of preferred frequency.
source: In all rats during awake periods, we found four clusters (Figure 1F) that differed significantly from the other clusters in terms of preferred frequency (p < 0.001, F3, 210 (gamma states)=1160.02, one-way ANOVA repeated Measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for six comparisons)
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (ANOVA and paired t-tests).

claim: The four clusters differed significantly from each other in terms of theta phase.
source: In all rats during awake periods, we found four clusters (Figure 1F) that differed significantly from the other clusters in terms of preferred frequency (p < 0.001, F3, 210 (gamma states)=1160.02, one-way ANOVA repeated Measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for six comparisons) and/or theta phase (Parametric Watson-Williams multi-sample test (Berens, 2009); q < 0.05, FDR correction for six comparisons)
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Watson-Williams test).

claim: Slow gamma (S-gamma) has a gravity frequency of 36.07±5.38 Hz during awake periods.
source: (1) a low frequency cluster (gravity frequency, GF = 36.07±5.38 Hz, n = 71, Table 1), which is denoted as slow gamma (S-gamma).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data analysis.

claim: Medium gamma (M-gamma) has a gravity frequency of 99.12±17.15 Hz during awake periods.
source: (2) a medium-frequency cluster (GF = 99.12±17.15 Hz, n = 71, Table 1) denoted as medium gamma (M-gamma)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data analysis.

claim: Early fast gamma (EF-gamma) has a gravity frequency of 127.72±11.28 Hz and a preferred phase of -2.57±0.83 radians during awake periods.
source: (3) a high-frequency cluster (GF = 127.72±11.28, n = 71, Table 1) with a preferred phase early in the theta cycle (-2.57±0.83 radians, n = 71, Table 1) denoted as early fast gamma (EF-gamma)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data analysis.

claim: Late fast gamma (LF-gamma) has a gravity frequency of 131.83±8.80 Hz and a preferred phase of 2.12±0.77 radians during awake periods.
source: (4) a high-frequency cluster (GF = 131.83±8.80, n = 71, Table 1) with a preferred phase late in the theta cycle (2.12±0.77 radians, n = 71, Table 1) denoted as late fast gamma (LF-gamma).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data analysis.

claim: The phase-difference between EF- and LF-gammas was around one quarter of a theta cycle.
source: The phase-difference between EF- and LF-gammas was around one quarter of a theta cycle when one considers that phase is cyclic.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured phase values.

claim: Four similar TG states were found during both theta dominated awake behavior and REM sleep.
source: Thus, we found four similar TG states during both theta dominated awake behavior and REM sleep.
evidence: This is a summary finding comparing awake and REM data.

claim: Almost all intra-cluster correlations were higher than the maximum inter-cluster correlations.
source: Almost all intra-cluster correlations were higher than the maximum inter-cluster correlations (the highest of the three inter-cluster correlations for each theta cycle; see Materials and methods) and on more than 50% of theta cycles intra-cluster correlations were 0.15 higher than the maximum inter-cluster correlations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This finding is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: On more than 50% of theta cycles, intra-cluster correlations were 0.15 higher than the maximum inter-cluster correlations.
source: Almost all intra-cluster correlations were higher than the maximum inter-cluster correlations (the highest of the three inter-cluster correlations for each theta cycle; see Materials and methods) and on more than 50% of theta cycles intra-cluster correlations were 0.15 higher than the maximum inter-cluster correlations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This finding is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Most theta cycles could be clearly classified into one specific TG state.
source: In other words, the FPP of those theta cycles were much more similar to its TG state than the other three states. This suggests that most, but not all, theta cycles could be clearly classified into one specific TG state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis results.

claim: Around 20% of theta cycles had a difference between intra- and maximum inter-cluster correlation that was close to zero (less than 0.05).
source: Around 20% of theta cycles had a difference between intra- and maximum inter-cluster correlation that was close to zero, specifically less than 0.05 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), showing that those samples share some similarities with at least two TG states.
evidence: This finding is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Some individual theta cycles share similarities with at least two TG states.
source: Around 20% of theta cycles had a difference between intra- and maximum inter-cluster correlation that was close to zero, specifically less than 0.05 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), showing that those samples share some similarities with at least two TG states.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis results.

claim: The four TG states are distinct from each other, while some individual theta cycles have features of multiple TG states.
source: Overall, our results suggest that the four TG states are distinct from each other, while some individual theta cycles have features of multiple TG states.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the correlation analysis.

claim: Cross-validation accuracy across channels or animals was generally above chance levels (25%) but highly variable, ranging from 0.30 to 0.96.
source: The cross validation was in general above chance levels (25% because a given theta cycle could be in four states), but highly variable ranging from 0.30 to 0.96 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5 top panel).
evidence: This finding is supported by the cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The network remained in the same state less than half of the time, showing that CA1 undergoes rapid TG state shifting.
source: First, we found rapid switches between different TG states with transition probabilities ranging from 0.15 to 0.36 and the probability of remaining in the same state ranging from 0.15 to 0.49 (Figure 2B,C; Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3). Thus, the network remained in the same state less than half of the time showing for the first time that CA1 undergoes rapid TG state shifting.
evidence: This finding is supported by the Markov chain analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Transition probabilities between different TG states ranged from 0.15 to 0.36.
source: First, we found rapid switches between different TG states with transition probabilities ranging from 0.15 to 0.36 and the probability of remaining in the same state ranging from 0.15 to 0.49 (Figure 2B,C; Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by the Markov chain analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The probability of remaining in the same state ranged from 0.15 to 0.49.
source: First, we found rapid switches between different TG states with transition probabilities ranging from 0.15 to 0.36 and the probability of remaining in the same state ranging from 0.15 to 0.49 (Figure 2B,C; Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by the Markov chain analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The occurrence of S-gamma states decreased when animals ran in a track compared to pre- and post-track awake periods.
source: We found the occurrence of S-gamma states as well as transitions from all states to S-gamma decreased when animals ran in a track compared to pre- and post-track awake periods (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2AB, the first column; p < 0.001, F38, 266 (TG states transition parameters × session)=11.07, two-way ANOVA repeated measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for 60 comparisons).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Transitions from all states to S-gamma decreased when animals ran in a track compared to pre- and post-track awake periods.
source: We found the occurrence of S-gamma states as well as transitions from all states to S-gamma decreased when animals ran in a track compared to pre- and post-track awake periods (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2AB, the first column; p < 0.001, F38, 266 (TG states transition parameters × session)=11.07, two-way ANOVA repeated measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for 60 comparisons).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both the occurrence of and transitions to M-gamma and EF-gamma were significantly enhanced when animals ran in the track compared to pre- and post-track sessions.
source: In contrast, both the occurrence of and transitions to M-gamma and EF-gamma were significantly enhanced when animals ran in the track compared to pre- and post-track sessions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Occurrences of M-gamma as well as S/M/EF-gamma→M-gamma transitions were enhanced during track running.
source: Occurrences of M-gamma as well as S/M/EF-gamma→M-gamma transitions were enhanced (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2AB, the second column; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for 60 comparisons).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EF-gamma occurrence and EF-gamma→EF-gamma transition were higher in the track.
source: EF-gamma occurrence and EF-gamma→EF-gamma transition were also higher in the track (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2AB, the third column).
evidence: This finding is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no difference in the transition matrix and occurrence of TG-states over early, middle, and late trials as the track became less novel.
source: However, there was no difference in the transition matrix and occurrence of TG-states over these early, middle, and late trials as the track became less novel (p = 0.462, F2, 14 (course) = 0.82; p = 0.112, F38, 266 (TG states transition parameters × course) = 1.32; two-way ANOVA repeated Measures; paired t-test, q > 0.1, FDR correction for 60 comparisons).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: During REM periods, no significant differences in state occurrence or transitions were found between pre- and post-track periods using a strong significance threshold.
source: During REM periods, we compared the occurrence of each state and state transition in the home cage before and after navigation in a novel environment (note that there are no REM periods during the track session). We found no significant differences using a strong significance threshold (paired t-test, q > 0.05, FDR correction for 20 comparisons).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Using a weaker significance threshold, decreased S-gamma→S-gamma transitions and increased S-gamma→LF-gamma transitions were found during REM after track running.
source: Using a weaker significance threshold (paired t-test, q < 0.1, FDR correction for 20 comparisons), we found decreased S-gamma→S-gamma transitions (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B; p = 0.008, t7 = 3.70, paired t-test) and increased S-gamma→LF-gamma transitions (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B; p = 0.007, t7 = -3.73, paired t-test).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At the beginning of REM both before and after track sessions, S-gamma occurred more frequently than the other states, persisting for approximately the first 20-30s of REM.
source: Interestingly, at the beginning of REM both before and after track sessions, S-gamma occurred more frequently than the other states, persisting for approximately the first 20-30s of REM (Figure 3; p < 0.001, F21, 609 (TG states × Time) = 4.69, two-way ANOVA repeated Measures).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3.

claim: As time progressed during REM, the occurrence of S-gamma decreased gradually and stabilized.
source: As time progressed, the occurrence of S-gamma decreased gradually, and stabilized.
evidence: This is an observation from the time-course analysis during REM.

claim: The other gamma states were stable across time during REM.
source: In contrast, the other gamma states were stable across time during REM (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the time-course analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: S-gamma is significantly higher than other theta-gamma coupling states during early REM.
source: These novel results show that S-gamma is significantly higher than other theta-gamma coupling states during early REM.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings about S-gamma during early REM.

claim: CA1-CA3 PPC showed a dominant peak in the slow gamma band (20-50 Hz) only during S-gamma states during exploration.
source: During exploration, we found a dominant peak in CA1-CA3 PPC in the slow gamma band (20-50 Hz) only during S-gamma states (Figure 4A top left; B left, blue arrow; p < 0.001, F213, 17040 (TG states × Frequency) = 44.80, two-way ANOVA repeated measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for 486 (81 Frequencies × 6 states pairs) comparisons), which was not present in CA1-EC PPC (Figure 4A top right; B middle and right).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: CA1-EC PPC showed a dominant peak in the medium gamma band (60-120 Hz) in M-gamma states in some recordings.
source: In contrast, CA1-EC PPC showed a dominant peak in the medium gamma band (60-120 Hz) in M-gamma states in some recordings (Figure 4A , top right).
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CA1-EC PPC showed higher values above 70Hz in M-, EF-, and LF-gamma states than in the S-gamma state.
source: Furthermore, combined data across all recordings revealed higher CA1-EC PPC above 70Hz in M-, EF-, and LF-gamma states than in the S-gamma state (Figure 4B middle, p < 0.001, F48, 3840 (TG states × Frequency) = 29.17, two-way ANOVA repeated measures; and Figure 4B right, p < 0.001, F78, 6240 (TG states × Frequency) = 40.13, two-way ANOVA repeated measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for 486 comparisons).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CA1-EC PPC was highest for the 60-80 Hz band and the 100-140 Hz band for M-gamma and EF-gamma states, respectively.
source: Particularly, CA1-EC PPC was highest for the 60-80 Hz band and the 100-140 Hz band for M-gamma and EF-gamma states, respectively (Figure 4B , middle and right, purple and green arrows).
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CA1-CA3 PPC during REM was the highest in S-gamma states in the slow gamma band.
source: As during awake behavior, CA1-CA3 PPC during REM was the highest in S-gamma states in the slow gamma band (Figure 4C left, p < 0.001, F21, 1680 (GT states × Frequency) = 10.48, two-way ANOVA repeated measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for 486 comparisons), however it is important to note that this data is drawn from one session in one animal.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4C, but is limited to one animal.

claim: CA1-EC PPC during REM showed peaks in 40-70 Hz within the M-gamma state.
source: CA1-EC PPC (four sessions from three animals) showed peaks in 40-70 Hz within the M-gamma state (Figure 4C top right), which was higher than the other three states although it was not significant (Figure 4D right, purple arrow).
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: S-gamma states had the strongest CA3-CA1 PPC in the slow gamma band in both REM and awake periods.
source: To summarize, S-gamma states had the strongest CA3-CA1 PPC in the slow gamma band in both REM and awake periods.
evidence: This is a summary of the PPC findings for S-gamma.

claim: EC-CA1 PPC was strongest in M-gamma states and EF-gamma states in the medium and high gamma bands, respectively.
source: In contrast, EC-CA1 PPC was strongest in M-gamma states and EF-gamma states in the medium and high gamma bands, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of the PPC findings for M-gamma and EF-gamma.

claim: EC-CA1 PPC showed the lowest values in medium and high gamma band during S-gamma states during awake and REM periods.
source: EC-CA1 PPC also showed the lowest values in medium and high gamma band during S-gamma states during awake and REM periods.
evidence: This is a summary of the PPC findings for S-gamma.

claim: The four TG states in CA1 differ in their phase synchrony with CA3 and EC.
source: Together, these results show that these four TG states in CA1 differ in their phase synchrony with CA3 and EC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the PPC analysis.

claim: The stronger CA3-CA1 synchrony during S-gamma and EC-CA1 synchrony during M-gamma are comparable with previous findings.
source: The stronger CA3-CA1 synchrony during S-gamma and EC-CA1 synchrony during M-gamma are comparable with previous findings (Colgin et al., 2009), that originally identified slow and medium gammas (which were called slow and fast gammas in that publication).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior research.

claim: Stronger EC-CA1 synchrony during EF-gamma and the difference between EF- and LF-gamma synchrony has not previously been reported.
source: However, stronger EC-CA1 synchrony during EF-gamma and the difference between EF- and LF-gamma synchrony has not previously been reported.
evidence: This statement identifies novel findings not reported in prior research.

claim: Neurons fired at lower rates in the S-gamma state for both interneurons and putative pyramidal cells.
source: Neurons fired at lower rates in the S-gamma state for both interneurons and putative pyramidal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Interneurons showed significantly higher spike-field phase synchrony than pyramidal cells in the theta band as well as slow and medium gamma bands.
source: Across all theta cycles, interneurons showed significantly higher spike-field phase synchrony than pyramidal cells in the theta band as well as slow and medium gamma bands, represented by their higher spike-LFP PPC values (Figure 5A)
evidence: This finding is supported by PPC analysis and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Pyramidal cells showed higher PPC values in the high gamma band than interneurons.
source: while pyramidal cells showed higher PPC values in the high gamma band (Figure 5A).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Pyramidal cells showed almost no difference in spike-LFP PPCs across TG states.
source: When we calculated PPCs for each TG state, we found pyramidal cells showed almost no difference in spike-LFP PPCs across states (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Interneurons had significantly higher PPCs in S-gamma states in the slow gamma band.
source: In contrast, interneurons had significantly higher PPCs in S-gamma states in the slow gamma band (Figure 5B)
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Significant differences in interneurons' PPCs in the medium gamma band were found across TG states.
source: and we found significant differences in interneurons' PPCs in the medium gamma band across TG states (Figure 5B).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Peak firing rate of place cells was lower in the S-gamma state.
source: Peak firing rate (p<0.001, F3, 423 (TG states)=65.75, one-way ANOVA repeated measures) and spatial information (p<0.001, F3, 423 (TG states)=30.99, one-way ANOVA repeated Measures) were also lower in the S-gamma state (Figure 5CD; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for six comparisons).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Spatial information of place cells was lower in the S-gamma state.
source: Peak firing rate (p<0.001, F3, 423 (TG states)=65.75, one-way ANOVA repeated measures) and spatial information (p<0.001, F3, 423 (TG states)=30.99, one-way ANOVA repeated Measures) were also lower in the S-gamma state (Figure 5CD; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for six comparisons).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: More S-gamma occurred when animals did not move.
source: We found more S-gamma when animals did not move (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Animal speed did not seem to account for differences in cells' firing properties across TG states.
source: Furthermore, animal speed did not seem to account for differences in cells' firing properties across TG states (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Low spatial information (<1 bits/theta cycle) was found in the occurrence of TG state events.
source: Additionally, we found low spatial information (<1 bits/theta cycle with 67% of having <0.1 bits/theta) in the occurrence of TG state events, for periods when animals ran faster than 5 cm/s, the same criteria used for calculating the spatial information of place cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The spatial preference of TG states is much lower than that of place cells.
source: These results show that the spatial preference of TG states is much lower than that of place cells (>1.2 bits/spike for more than 90% of the cells).
evidence: This is a comparison between TG state spatial information and place cell spatial information.

claim: S-gamma has lower spatial information and is more likely to occur when animals are moving slowly.
source: Furthermore, these results show that S-gamma has lower spatial information and is more likely to occur when animals are moving slowly.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about S-gamma and animal movement.

claim: The phase-precession slope was lower in each TG state than when all spikes in all states were included.
source: Generally, because separating spikes into their respective TG states reduced the number of spikes, the phase-position regression slope (p=0.002, F4, 564 (gamma states)=4.33, one way ANOVA repeated measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for 10 comparisons;) and phase-position correlation (p<0.001, F4, 564 (gamma states)=7.73, one way ANOVA repeated measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for 10 comparisons) were lower in each state than when all spikes in all states were included (Figure 5FG, top).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5F and 5G.

claim: The phase-position correlation was lower in each TG state than when all spikes in all states were included.
source: Generally, because separating spikes into their respective TG states reduced the number of spikes, the phase-position regression slope (p=0.002, F4, 564 (gamma states)=4.33, one way ANOVA repeated measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for 10 comparisons;) and phase-position correlation (p<0.001, F4, 564 (gamma states)=7.73, one way ANOVA repeated measures; paired t-test, q < 0.05, FDR correction for 10 comparisons) were lower in each state than when all spikes in all states were included (Figure 5FG, top).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5F and 5G.

claim: Phase precession in S-gamma states showed a trend of being weaker than the other three TG states.
source: Comparing the TG states to each other, phase precession in S-gamma states showed a trend of being weaker than the other three, although it was not significantly different (p>0.05, paired t-test) except for the phase-position correlation with LF-gamma (Figure 5G, top).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 5G.

claim: After controlling for spike counts, no difference in the slope of phase precession was found across TG states.
source: For the slope of phase precession, after controlling for spike counts, no difference (p=0.14, F4, 564 (gamma states)=1.75, one way ANOVA repeated measures) was found in S-gamma (p=0.71, t141 = 0.38 paired t-test), EF-gamma (p=0.73, t141 = 0.35 paired t-test) and LF-gamma (p=0.22, t141 = 1.23 paired t-test) compared to raw values in which no spikes were deleted.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis after controlling for spike counts.

claim: Controlling for spike counts significantly affected phase-position correlations.
source: Controlling for spike counts significantly affected phase-position correlations (p=0.04, F4, 564 (gamma states)=2.48, one-way ANOVA repeated measures).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Phase-position correlations were significantly higher in M-gamma after controlling for spike counts.
source: Phase-position correlations were significantly higher in M-gamma (p=0.02, t141 = 2.42 paired t-test; q < 0.1, FDR correction for 10 comparisons) and LF-gamma (p=0.01, t141 = 2.54 paired t-test; q < 0.1, FDR correction for 10 comparisons, Figure 5G, bottom).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Phase-position correlations were significantly higher in LF-gamma after controlling for spike counts.
source: Phase-position correlations were significantly higher in M-gamma (p=0.02, t141 = 2.42 paired t-test; q < 0.1, FDR correction for 10 comparisons) and LF-gamma (p=0.01, t141 = 2.54 paired t-test; q < 0.1, FDR correction for 10 comparisons, Figure 5G, bottom).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Spikes from M and LF-gamma made a significant contribution to theta phase precession.
source: These results show that spikes from M and LF-gamma made a significant contribution to theta phase precession.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the phase precession analysis.

claim: Place cell firing in M-, EF-, and LF-gamma states contributed to spatial tuning significantly more than in S-gamma.
source: Thus, we show for the first time that place cell firing in M-, EF-, and LF-gamma states contributed to spatial tuning significantly more than in S-gamma; while M- and LF-gamma contributed to phase precession significantly more than other states.
evidence: This is a summary of the spatial coding findings.

claim: M- and LF-gamma contributed to phase precession significantly more than other states.
source: Thus, we show for the first time that place cell firing in M-, EF-, and LF-gamma states contributed to spatial tuning significantly more than in S-gamma; while M- and LF-gamma contributed to phase precession significantly more than other states.
evidence: This is a summary of the phase precession findings.

claim: The study used k-means clustering with k determined by community clustering to produce robust clustering.
source: In short, we used k-means clustering with k determined by community clustering to produce robust clustering.
evidence: This describes the clustering methodology used.

claim: The S-gamma state detected in both awake and REM periods is dominant in the range of 30–50 Hz and nested in the descending phase of pyramidal theta, which is consistent with slow gamma reported previously.
source: The S-gamma state we detected in both awake and REM periods, is dominant in the range of 30–50 Hz and nested in the descending phase of pyramidal theta, which is consistent with slow gamma reported previously (Colgin et al., 2009; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior research.

claim: Stronger CA3-CA1 coupling in 20–50 Hz was found in S-gamma states, as reported previously.
source: Additionally, we found stronger CA3-CA1 coupling in 20–50 Hz in S-gamma states, as reported previously (Colgin et al., 2009; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2016; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior research.

claim: The M-gamma state falls into the frequency range of 60–120 Hz nested in the peak of pyramidal theta, which corresponds to medium gamma reported previously.
source: The M-gamma state we found falls into the frequency range of 60–120 Hz nested in the peak of pyramidal theta, which corresponds to medium gamma reported previously, first identified as fast gamma in Colgin et al. (2009) and later called medium or fast gamma (Colgin, 2015b; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2016).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior research.

claim: Higher EC-CA1 coupling in 60–80 Hz or 40–70 Hz was observed in M-gamma states than the other three states during awake periods and REM periods, respectively.
source: We observed higher EC-CA1 coupling in 60–80 Hz or 40–70 Hz in M-gamma states than the other three states during awake periods and REM periods, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the PPC analysis.

claim: The EF-gamma and LF-gamma identified fell into the >120 Hz range but occurred at different phases of theta.
source: Finally, the EF-gamma and LF-gamma we identified fell into the >120 Hz range but occurred at different phases of theta with EF-gamma at the beginning of the theta ascending phase and LF-gamma at the late descending phase.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of EF-gamma and LF-gamma.

claim: Both EF- and LF-gamma are similar to fast gamma reported nesting in the trough of pyramidal theta but are quite distinct from each other in theta phase.
source: Both EF- and LF-gamma are similar to fast gamma reported nesting in the trough of pyramidal theta but are quite distinct from each other in theta phase (Amemiya and Redish, 2018; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2016).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior research.

claim: Higher EC-CA1 coupling was observed in EF-gamma than in LF-gamma.
source: In addition, higher EC-CA1 coupling was observed in EF-gamma than in LF-gamma.
evidence: This is a finding from the PPC analysis.

claim: EF- and LF-gamma are two sub-types of fast gamma not previously differentiated.
source: Together, these results suggest that EF- and LF-gamma are distinct and that they are two sub-types of fast gamma not previously differentiated.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Frequent cycle-to-cycle switching between different TG states was found, showing that the hippocampus can rapidly shift between these different proposed functional states.
source: Generally, we found frequent cycle-to-cycle switching between different TG states showing that the hippocampus can rapidly shift between these different proposed functional states.
evidence: This is a summary of the state transition findings.

claim: Sub-second dynamic changes of TG states suggest that not only individual theta cycles but also cycle-by-cycle transitions should be further studied to understand hippocampal function.
source: These sub-second dynamic changes of TG states suggest that not only individual theta cycles but also cycle-by-cycle transitions should be further studied to understand hippocampal function.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings.

claim: M-gamma but not S-gamma fit with expected roles in sensory processing with dominant EC-CA1 coupling in the medium gamma band.
source: Consistent with these studies, we found M-gamma but not S-gamma fit with these expected roles in sensory processing with dominant EC-CA1 coupling in the medium gamma band.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior research.

claim: Significantly decreased S-gamma and increased M- and EF-gamma were found during exploration of a novel environment, supporting the notion that M- and EF-gamma but not S-gamma reflect sensory processing.
source: We found significantly decreased S-gamma and increased M- and EF-gamma, supporting the notion that M- and EF-gamma but not S-gamma reflect sensory processing that is expected during exploration of a novel environment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral state findings.

claim: CA1-EC4/5 coupling was significantly stronger in the high gamma band during EF-gamma and significantly weaker during S-gamma than other states during waking.
source: During waking, CA1-EC4/5 coupling was significantly stronger in the high gamma band during EF-gamma and was significantly weaker during S-gamma than other states, with M- and LF-gamma in between.
evidence: This is a finding from the PPC analysis.

claim: The results could arise from stronger CA1-EC4/5 coupling during EF-gamma or they could indicate that EF- and LF-gamma undergo different transformations within CA1.
source: These results could arise from stronger CA1-EC4/5 coupling during EF-gamma or they could indicate that EF- and LF-gamma undergo different transformations within CA1.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: M-gamma may also play a role in CA3-CA1 interactions, which has not been reported previously.
source: These results suggest that M-gamma may also play a role in CA3-CA1 interactions, which has not been reported previously (Cabral et al., 2014; Colgin, 2015a; Newman et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2014; Tort et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings that differs from prior research.

claim: As animals run faster, the frequency of gamma oscillations also tends to be faster.
source: Prior work revealed that as animals run faster, the frequency of gamma oscillations also tends to be faster (Ahmed and Mehta, 2012; Colgin, 2015a; Kemere et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement references prior research.

claim: S-gamma was more likely to occur when animals moved slowly.
source: Consistent with these papers, we observed S-gamma was more likely to occur when animals moved slowly.
evidence: This is a finding from the speed analysis.

claim: The relationship between gamma power and animal speed was stronger in a novel environment than in a familiar environment.
source: Kemere et al. further showed that the relationship between gamma power and animal speed was stronger in a novel environment than in a familiar environment (Kemere et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement references prior research.

claim: S-gamma is significantly higher than other TG states during early REM, which could point to a role for S-gamma in memory consolidation or homeostasis.
source: Here, for the first time, we show that S-gamma is significantly higher than other TG states during early REM. This could point to a role for S-gamma in memory consolidation or homeostasis (Borbély, 1982; Borbély et al., 2016; Tononi and Cirelli, 2014; Tononi and Cirelli, 2003; Watson et al., 2016), as both are hypothesized functions of REM sleep.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the REM findings in the context of prior hypotheses.

claim: Slightly decreased S-gamma to S-gamma transitions and enhanced S-gamma to LF-gamma transitions were observed over the entire REM period after navigation in a novel environment.
source: While S-gamma dominated during early REM, we also observed slightly decreased S-gamma to S-gamma transitions and enhanced S-gamma to LF-gamma transitions over the entire REM period after navigation in a novel environment.
evidence: This is a finding from the REM state transition analysis.

claim: These interactions of S-gamma and LF-gamma could be related to synapse re-scaling according to the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis.
source: These interactions of S-gamma and LF-gamma could be related to synapse re-scaling according to the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis (Borbély, 1982; Borbély et al., 2016; Tononi and Cirelli, 2014; Tononi and Cirelli, 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in the context of a hypothesis from prior research.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons participate in the generation of gamma oscillations widely in the brain.
source: Inhibitory interneurons participate in the generation of gamma oscillations widely in the brain (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).
evidence: This statement references prior research.

claim: Distinct spike field phase synchrony patterns in interneurons were found during different TG states, indicating that these cells are differentially modulated in different gammas.
source: We found distinct spike field phase synchrony patterns in interneurons during different TG states, indicating that these cells are differentially modulated in different gammas.
evidence: This is a finding from the spike-field PPC analysis.

claim: Interneurons were more strongly modulated at 20–60 Hz during S-gamma states and at 60–120 Hz during M-, EF-, and LF-gamma states.
source: Separating each TG state, interneurons were more strongly modulated at 20–60 Hz during S-gamma states and at 60–120 Hz during M-, EF-, and LF-gamma states, while pyramidal cell modulation did not vary significantly from one TG state to another.
evidence: This is a finding from the spike-field PPC analysis.

claim: Pyramidal cell modulation did not vary significantly from one TG state to another.
source: Separating each TG state, interneurons were more strongly modulated at 20–60 Hz during S-gamma states and at 60–120 Hz during M-, EF-, and LF-gamma states, while pyramidal cell modulation did not vary significantly from one TG state to another.
evidence: This is a finding from the spike-field PPC analysis.

claim: Differential effects on interneuron and pyramidal cell firing may be because interneurons are more strongly driven by gammas from CA3 and EC, known local gamma generators.
source: These differential effects on interneuron and pyramidal cell firing may be because interneurons are more strongly driven by gammas from CA3 and EC, known local gamma generators (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2016; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2014; Somogyi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior research.

claim: Recent studies suggest phase precession varies across single traversals of an environment or in different theta-gamma coupling states.
source: Recent studies suggest phase precession varies across single traversals of an environment or in different theta-gamma coupling states (Amemiya and Redish, 2018; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement references prior research.

claim: Significantly weaker phase precession was found for spikes occurring in S-gamma than those in the other states.
source: We found significantly weaker phase precession for spikes occurring in S-gamma than those in the other states and higher phase precession for spikes occurring in M- and LF-gamma.
evidence: This is a finding from the phase precession analysis.

claim: Higher phase precession was found for spikes occurring in M- and LF-gamma.
source: We found significantly weaker phase precession for spikes occurring in S-gamma than those in the other states and higher phase precession for spikes occurring in M- and LF-gamma.
evidence: This is a finding from the phase precession analysis.

claim: Different TG states play distinct roles in hippocampal spatial coding.
source: Together these results suggest that different TG states play distinct roles in hippocampal spatial coding.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the spatial coding findings.
